extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and higher education institutions), Title IX coordinators/compliance officers, policymakers, and stakeholders commenting on Title IX rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory preamble and Regulatory Impact Analysis for the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations, describing substantive rules (retaliation, confidentiality, grievance procedures), the rationale for changes, and the methodological approach and limits for the cost/benefit analysis. Intended to guide recipients on compliance and to explain the Department's evidentiary and analytic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation prohibition (§106.71)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients and other persons are prohibited from intimidating, threatening, coercing, or discriminating against any individual for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX or its implementing regulations, or because the individual has made a report or complaint, testified, assisted, participated, or refused to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaliation includes charges against an individual for code of conduct violations that do not involve sex discrimination or sexual harassment but arise out of the same facts or circumstances as a report or complaint of sex discrimination or sexual harassment. This provision is intended to be more precise than prior guidance (e.g., withdrawn 2014 Q&A) and applies regardless of whether the alleged retaliatory act involves non-sex-related code violations if motivated to interfere with Title IX rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of identities in Title IX processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must keep confidential the identity of any individual who has made a report or complaint of sex discrimination (including a formal complaint of sexual harassment), any complainant, any individual reported to be the perpetrator, any respondent, and any witness, except as permitted by FERPA, as required by law, or to the extent necessary to carry out the purposes of Part 106 (including investigations, hearings, or judicial proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality exceptions are limited to FERPA permissions/statutory requirements and to what is necessary for conducting the Title IX process. The rule places an affirmative obligation on recipients to maintain confidentiality subject to those narrow exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural vehicle for retaliation complaints (§106.8(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints alleging retaliation may be filed according to the grievance procedures for sex discrimination that recipients are required to adopt under §106.8(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation explicitly ties retaliation complaints to the same grievance process used for sex discrimination, clarifying that reporting retaliation to the recipient should follow the formal grievance procedures rather than informal or unspecified channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment exercise not retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercise of rights under the First Amendment does not constitute retaliation under these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether conduct is retaliation, recipients must not treat protected speech/expression protected by the First Amendment as retaliatory conduct simply because it is unpopular or related to the underlying facts; First Amendment activity is explicitly exempted from retaliation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materially false statements in bad faith exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Charging an individual with a code of conduct violation for making a materially false statement in bad faith in the course of a grievance proceeding under the regulations implementing Title IX does not constitute retaliation; however, a determination regarding responsibility alone is not sufficient to conclude that any party made a materially false statement in bad faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may pursue conduct rules for knowingly false and bad-faith statements made during grievance proceedings without that action being treated as retaliation, but must not presume bad faith simply from an adverse finding—bad-faith determinations require separate, sufficient evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each regulation is designed to operate independently; a potential invalidity of one provision should not affect the remainder of the provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severability clauses are added at the end of each subpart of Part 106 (specified in §§106.9, 106.18, 106.24, 106.46, 106.62, and 106.72) to make clear the Department's intent that each provision is distinct and independently valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis — exclude costs of underlying incidents absent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department did not include costs associated with underlying incidents of sexual harassment and assault in its cost estimates because there is insufficient evidence that the final regulations would affect the underlying number of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA cost estimates should not incorporate societal or victim costs from the underlying misconduct (healthcare, lost earnings, dropout consequences) unless there is rigorous evidence linking the regulatory change to changes in incident rates; the Department used available analyses (e.g., 2011 Dear Colleague Letter analysis) and found insufficient evidence to attribute such effects to the final regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Impact Analysis — include costs of providing supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised its cost estimates to include the costs of recipients offering supportive measures to complainants pursuant to §106.44(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the regulations require recipients to offer supportive measures, RIA must account for the direct costs to recipients of providing such measures (noting that the regulations define supportive measures as offered without fee or charge to complainants and respondents). The Department nonetheless declines to include uncertain savings to complainants from these measures absent clear data on take-up and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures offered without fee (§106.44(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures, as defined in §106.30 and required by §106.44(a), are offered without fee or charge to the complainant or the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule element affects both compliance obligations and RIA cost accounting (costs fall to recipients, not complainants/respondents). The Department included recipient costs for offering supportive measures but did not treat them as costs borne by complainants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Clery Act data and correlation assumption in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department used Clery Act reports (Forcible Sex Offenses 2007–2013) to analyze potential effects of prior guidance and assumed that Clery Act reports are uniformly correlated with the underlying rate of sexual harassment and assault, while acknowledging major limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses relying on Clery Act data must explicitly state and justify the correlation assumption and discuss how reporting behavior changes or institutional reporting practices could bias results; inability to validate the correlation is a major limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling guidance for RIA (specification and controls)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's analytic specifications included regressions with a POST dummy for post-guidance period, year and year-squared terms to allow non-linear trends, enrollment, institutional characteristics (control and level), and robbery counts as a control for general campus crime; both aggregate and campus-level panel regressions were estimated using OLS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA analyses should allow for non-linear time trends (e.g., quadratic in year), control for enrollment and institutional characteristics (public/private, two-year/four-year), and include controls for general crime trends (robbery) to avoid misattributing effects. The Department also notes alternative specifications (e.g., Tobit) could be considered but did not believe they would change the substantive conclusion given their data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of RIA limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The RIA must candidly disclose limitations including potential omitted variables, quality and completeness of Clery Act data, inability to observe actual underlying incidents, changes in reporting behavior by victims or institutions, the assumption of correlation between reports and incidents, appropriateness of controls, and model specification choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department lists these limitations explicitly as reasons for caution in interpreting results and for declining to include certain long-range or causally distant cost estimates. RIAs should similarly enumerate analytic and data limitations and avoid overreaching conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude temporally/cause-distant speculative benefits/costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to include in the cost estimates effects that are temporally or causally distant from implementation (e.g., lost future tax revenue from lower lifetime earnings, reduced future health care costs) because they are difficult and impractical to quantify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIAs should omit speculative, long-run downstream economic effects where causal chains are tenuous and quantification would be unreliable; focus on more immediate, attributable costs and benefits that can be reasonably estimated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on comment-responsive revision of assumptions and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to comments, the Department revised RIA assumptions and estimates — adding a new recipient category, updating assumptions about the number of annual investigations, increasing estimated time burdens for certain activities, and adding new cost categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory analyses should be responsive to substantive public comments and update modeling assumptions, category definitions, and cost elements where justified by credible information received through the notice-and-comment process.
